newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition, SPD hope for tax deal by Easter.
newsitem.headline: German coalition, SPD hope for tax deal by Easter.

text.p: Leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's German coalition and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Wednesday they hoped to thrash out a compromise on tax reforms before parliament's Easter break.
Speaking ahead of a tax summit between Kohl and SPD chiefs next Monday, leaders on both sides said it would be possible to agree main points of the tax changes by the end of March.

SPD chief whip Peter Struck said he did not expect a quick deal to be reached at next Monday's talks, but added: "We must agree on the main points by Easter so that the reform can take effect at the start of 1998."
Coalition leaders on Tuesday approved a bill drafted by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to make tax cuts next year under a two-year plan to knock 30 billion marks off the total tax load.
A draft for the remaining tax changes to be made in 1999 will be ready next month.

The two sides are seeking a quick tax deal to help revive Germany's unemployment-hit economy. They also want to avoid lengthy wrangling in parliament -- where the SPD controls the upper house -- from dragging into the 1998 election campaign.
Hermann Otto Solms, tax negotiator for junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said he was open to SPD calls to bring as much of the tax reform forward to 1998 as possible.

Solms repeated his support for a cut in the top rate of income tax -- which under Waigel's plan would fall to 39 percent from 53 percent now. He warned that a smaller cut would leave a gap between income and corparate taxes which could violate Germany's constitution.
Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), called on the SPD to drop its delaying tactics if tax cuts are to be brought forward to 1998.
"I am not raising my hopes. The reform plans must not be watered down," he told reporters in Munich.

SPD chief whip Franz Muentefering told German Radio that his party had not taken a position on the top rate of income tax. But he ruled out coalition plans to finance a cut in the highest tax bracket by raising value-added tax or scrapping existing tax breaks for night, holiday and weekend shifts.
Both sides were deadlocked ahead of a parliamentary debate on Friday over government efforts to abolish a capital trading tax which has been blocked by the SPD.
Struck confirmed on Wednesday afternoon that the coalition had rejected an SPD proposal to postpone Friday's vote on scrapping the tax until after after next week's tax summit.
The SPD wants to link the abolition of the tax to restoring a wealth tax which was dropped at the end of 1996 after being ruled illegal by Germany's constitutional court.

Failure to agree would force the automatic imposition of the tax in eastern Germany. That, the government says, would put more people on the dole in a region where nearly one person in five is jobless.
